extracted.intended_audience: philanthropists, trustees, and administrators of charitable endowments and foundations
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and practical standards for creating, structuring, governing, and distributing large philanthropic gifts (endowments, pension funds, institutional foundations, relief funds) and for selecting officers/trustees and operating policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose clause for institutional endowments
rubrics_metrics.description: Deed of gift wording for the Carnegie Institution: "To encourage in the broadest and most liberal manner investigations, research and discovery, and the application of knowledge to the improvement of mankind; and, in particular, to conduct, endow and assist investigation in any department of science, literature or art, and to this end to coöperate with governments, universities, colleges, technical schools, learned societies, and individuals."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State a broad but explicit mission in the deed of gift that permits cooperation with public and private bodies; the quoted language illustrates an institutional-purpose clause that both defines scope and enables collaboration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select distinguished trustees and officers
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose eminent, capable persons to serve as trustees and officers: Carnegie consulted experts (Dr. Billings) and secured noted public figures (e.g., John Hay, Abram S. Hewitt, Elihu Root) as directors and presidents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use recognized leaders and technical advisers to lend expertise, credibility and wise governance; consult trusted subject-matter advisors when selecting institution presidents or directors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tie additional funding to demonstrated results
rubrics_metrics.description: Initial gift (ten million dollars in five per cent bonds) was later supplemented "to make the total cash value twenty-five millions of dollars, the additions being made upon record of results obtained."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make follow-on disbursements contingent on measurable outcomes or demonstrated progress to ensure funds are expanded only as the institution proves effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow trustees power to adapt objects for future suitability
rubrics_metrics.description: Carnegie gave trustees the right to change the objects of beneficence and modes of applying funds should they later decide original purposes were unsuitable; there was debate over whether a simple majority or two-thirds should be required: "I had proposed that a majority should have the power, but Lord Balfour suggested not less than two thirds. This was accepted... It is incorporated in all my large gifts."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include an amendment/variation clause in trusts/endowments allowing future trustees to adapt objectives; consider requiring a supermajority (e.g., two-thirds) as a prudent safeguard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design funds for pensions/support, not as incentives for risky acts
rubrics_metrics.description: On the Hero Fund Carnegie states many misunderstood its purpose as stimulating heroic action. He clarifies: "The fund is intended to pension or provide in the most suitable manner for the hero should he be disabled, or for those dependent upon him should he perish in his attempt to save others."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When creating reward or heroism-type funds, explicitly define them as compensatory/pension/support mechanisms rather than bounties intended to induce dangerous conduct; articulate intent in governing documents to avoid misinterpretation and perverse incentives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use local commissions/committees for cross‑national administration
rubrics_metrics.description: The Hero Fund was extended to many countries with local commissions; those commissions exchanged reports and corresponded with other national commissions to improve decision-making.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For international programs, establish locally-based, carefully chosen commissions that coordinate with peer bodies abroad and exchange reports to adapt best practices regionally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematize applications and graduate gifts to recipient size
rubrics_metrics.description: Carnegie developed a "printed schedule requiring answers to many questions" to be filled before action, and said the department "works admirably because we graduate the gift according to the size of the church."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement standardized application processes (questionnaires, schedules) and scale gift amounts to recipient capacity/size to ensure reasonable, sustainable allocations and administrative efficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require partial recipient contribution to ensure commitment
rubrics_metrics.description: Regarding church organs Carnegie required each congregation to pay one half of the desired new organ: "I therefore asked each congregation to pay one half of the desired new organ."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require matching or cost‑sharing (e.g., 50%) from beneficiaries to promote responsible spending, local buy-in, and continuing stewardship of donated assets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidential, discretionary private pensioning of deserving individuals
rubrics_metrics.description: On his private pension list Carnegie emphasizes privacy and selectivity: "There is no publicity about it. No one knows who is embraced. Not a word is ever breathed to others... Not one person have I ever placed upon the pension list that did not fully deserve assistance."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operate private pension or relief lists with strict confidentiality and careful vetting of recipients to preserve dignity and avoid public controversy; avoid publicity for individual grants unless expressly desired.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target aid where marginal benefit is greatest (smaller institutions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Carnegie explains he declined to enlarge rich universities and instead "confined myself to these [smaller institutions] and am satisfied that this was wise," arguing smaller colleges needed help more than large universities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize gifts to institutions or programs where philanthropic dollars produce the largest incremental impact, rather than further enlarging already well-endowed organizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordinate with other philanthropists and avoid harmful duplication
rubrics_metrics.description: Carnegie notes independent but overlapping efforts with Rockefeller's General Education Board and that "Coöperation was soon found to be much to our mutual advantage, and we now work in unison."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Engage in dialogue and coordination with other major funders to harmonize strategies, reduce duplication, and amplify collective impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appoint devoted, unpaid local managers where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Carnegie describes Charlie Taylor managing the Hero Fund and other pensions and taking no salary: "No salary for Charlie--not a cent would he ever take. He loves the work so much... He is the right man in the right place."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible, appoint committed local managers or volunteers who demonstrate devotion and integrity; compensation structures should reflect duties, but loyal, capable unpaid stewardship can be effective for some roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use naming rights strategically when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Carnegie used naming (e.g., 'Taylor Hall') to secure support and influence decisions: he offered funds conditioned upon naming; he discusses the use of names to honor friends and encourage giving.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider offering naming opportunities as part of gift terms to motivate beneficiary institutions or stakeholders, but weigh the reputational and ethical implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow flexibility in individual provisions to avoid stigma or improvidence
rubrics_metrics.description: When Booker Washington requested changing a clause that set aside a large fixed sum for support during life, Carnegie agreed to substitute the phrase 'only suitable provision' at Washington's request to avoid undue appearance of wealth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design individual benefactor clauses with flexibility (e.g., 'suitable provision' language) to respect recipients' dignity and local norms; be willing to amend fixed provisions where appropriate and with proper recordkeeping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select appropriate technologies/materials informed by technical experts
rubrics_metrics.description: Example: The survey ship 'Carnegie' was constructed of wood and bronze because bronze is non-magnetic and corrects compass-related errors in earlier iron/steel ships; this technical choice yielded corrected nautical charts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When funding technical projects, ensure material and design choices are informed by domain experts so the gift solves the technical problem (e.g., choose non-magnetic materials for magnetic-sensitivity tasks).

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish endowments and chairs to honor individuals and support disciplines
rubrics_metrics.description: Carnegie founded named chairs, libraries, and funds (e.g., Stanton Chair, Hanna Chair, John Hay Library, Elihu Root Foundation) to commemorate friends and support academic work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create named endowments and named facilities to memorialize individuals while directing sustained resources to specific academic disciplines or institutional needs; communicate intent and governance for such gifts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create targeted national funds for professions with low retirement security
rubrics_metrics.description: Carnegie established a fifteen‑million‑dollar pension fund for aged university professors (The Carnegie Endowment for the Advancement of Learning) because professors were often poorly paid and unable to save for old age.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design sector‑specific pension endowments where professions lack retirement security to preserve institutional quality and prevent retention of underperforming personnel due to lack of pension alternatives.
